title: What If the Most Strategic Thing You Did Today Was Nothing?
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Salinas argues that leaders have lost the ability to pause and that deliberately protecting margin, the space between limits and load, is a strategic act. He treats urgency as legitimate in seasons but destructive as a default, leading to burnout, blurry thinking and turnover in church and nonprofit settings. Margin, he says, is the modern currency of control over time, and he offers AI as one partial help, with prompts for meeting summaries, agenda ordering and draft critique, plus a guest comment about turning saved minutes into optionality. He is clear that there is no magic amount of margin and that it will not appear by default, and he proposes practical rhythms: question meeting invitations and keep a quiet midweek day. The AI section is brief and the argument is mostly reflective, but the margin framing and the two rhythms are usable for leaders.
points: Margin is defined as the space between limits and load, and leaders are urged to guard it in order to think clearly.
Urgency is acceptable in a season but corrosive as a default, because a leader without reserves cannot meet the next crisis.
AI can create margin by absorbing repetitive work, but it is explicitly only one part of the answer.
Declining meetings with no clear purpose and holding a no-meeting day build a team culture that protects deep work.
Starting small, with one hour or one boundary, is enough since there is no required amount of margin.
quotes: Margin is the space between your limits and your load. It’s the emotional, mental, and spiritual breathing room that allows you to think clearly, lead wisely, and stay grounded. Without it, even the most gifted leaders lose clarity, presence, and joy.

We say yes when we’re depleted. We schedule back-to-back-to-back meetings and call it productive. We stay in reaction mode instead of reflection mode. But leadership without margin is just stress management dressed up in strategy.

The problem isn’t urgency. It’s when urgency becomes the status quo. When all you do is respond, putting out fires, jumping from project to project, you’re trying to run a marathon at a 100-meter sprint pace. And we both know what that leads to: burnout, blurry thinking, high turnover, and no time to plan ahead.

When you use AI to handle the repetitive 80% of a task (things like research, sorting information, or drafting), you’re not just saving time, you’re creating margin. A task that once took 90 minutes might now take just 15, leaving you with 75 extra minutes. That margin is a kind of convertible currency you can reinvest wherever it pays the biggest dividends: sharpening your strategy, experimenting with new ideas, or simply taking a break so you return sharper. The real value isn’t just in the time saved, but in the 75 minutes of optionality you’ve gained, and what you choose to do with it.
Even 10% more breathing room in your week changes how you think, decide, and lead. Don’t wait until you have a full day off. Start with one reclaimed hour.
Margin rarely feels strategic in the moment. It may mean slowing a launch, skipping a meeting, or postponing something that looks productive.

If I get invited to a meeting without a clear reason I need to be there, I ask. If the answer is “just in case” or “FYI,” I usually decline or catch the recording at 2x speed later. Do this enough and it builds a boundary. And more importantly, a culture.
